lesson.title: Take exactly the text you need

steps.headline: A string's positions start at 0, and a slice takes the characters from the start up to, but not including, the stop.

lead.text: In 'CRAYON', C is at position 0, R at 1, A at 2. word[1:3] takes positions 1 and 2. A negative position counts back from the end, so word[-1] is the last character.
The start is included. The stop is not.
Take the characters from position 2 up to, but not including, position 5.

reveal.text: You counted positions 2, 3 and 4. The stop was not included, so the length of a slice is just the stop minus the start.

steps.headline: A string method returns a new string. It never changes the original.

lead.text: Strings cannot be changed in place. name.strip() removes spaces at both ends, and name.upper() makes capitals, but each hands back a new string. Store it if you want to keep it.

steps.headline: Take the last four characters of 'HARVEST'.

workedSteps.text: A negative start counts back from the end. Four back from the end is -4.
Leaving the stop empty means: carry on to the end of the string.
Positions start at 0. The slice starts at position 1 and stops before position 5.
Count the positions from 1 up to, but not including, 5. How many is that?

lead.text: Inside a Python string, backslash-n stands for a newline. It is two keystrokes in the source and one character in the string.

reveal.text: Each escape counts once in len. Two characters of source became one character of text, so counting what you see on the page is not enough.

lead.text: A slice whose bounds run past the end simply stops at the end. A single position past the end is different: it raises an IndexError.

reveal.text: A slice never complains: it returns whatever lies inside its bounds, which here is nothing. That makes slices safe on short input, where a single index would fail.

lesson.orientation: Use zero-based indexing, slice boundaries and string methods.
lesson.reviewLabel: Take exactly the text you need
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea with a new input.

blocks.text: A ruler starts at 0. A pencil's tip lines up with the 2 cm mark and its other end with the 5 cm mark.

intro.promise: By the end you'll count positions from zero, cut text with [start:stop], and know which string methods change the original.

recap.keyIdea: Positions count from zero. A slice includes its start and excludes its stop, and a string method hands back a new string rather than changing the old one.

blocks.text: You measured the pencil at 3 cm, then found 'ORCHARD'[2:5] has 3 characters. You also found that a slice past the end of 'AB' leaves 0.

recap.nextHook: Next: lists, where one name can quietly point at the same collection as another.

hints: Subtract the start from the stop.
The start is included and the stop is not.
Count positions beginning at 2 and ending just before 5.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The slice includes positions 2, 3 and 4: 'CHA', three characters.

questions.onCorrect: 3. The slice has positions 2, 3 and 4. Its length is the stop minus the start.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts position 5 as well. The stop is not included.
That is the stop position. The question asks for the length of the slice.

questions.prompt: After name = '  hill  ', what does name.strip() do if its result is ignored?
hints: Strings cannot be changed in place.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: strip returns a new string. Without assignment, name still refers to the original padded text.

questions.onCorrect: It leaves name unchanged. strip returns a new string, and nothing stored it.

misconceptions.feedback: That would change the string in place. Strings cannot be changed; strip returns a new one.
Nothing is deleted. name still refers to the original text.

questions.prompt: A Python string is written as the letter a, then backslash-n, then the letter b. What is its len?
hints: A newline escape represents one character.
The escape stands for a line break inside the string.
Count a, the newline and b as individual characters.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: There is one a, one newline and one b: three characters.

questions.onCorrect: 3. Backslash-n is a single newline character, so a, newline and b make three.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts the backslash and the n separately. Together they stand for one newline character.

hints: Where does the slice start, and how long is the string?
Position 5 is past the end of a two-character string.
A slice keeps only what lies inside its bounds.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The slice starts beyond the available characters, so it is an empty string with 0 characters.

questions.onCorrect: 0. The slice starts beyond the end, so nothing lies inside it. It returns an empty string.

misconceptions.feedback: That returns the whole string. The slice starts after its last character.
That is the gap between the bounds. A slice only keeps characters that exist.

questions.prompt: How many characters remain after ' DATA '.strip()?
hints: Count after trimming the outside spaces.
strip removes spaces at both ends only.
Count the letters between the spaces.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Removing the leading and trailing spaces leaves DATA, which has four characters.

questions.onCorrect: 4. strip returns DATA, with no spaces at either end.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts the original string. The question is about the stripped result.

hints: A negative start counts back from the end.
An omitted stop means the end of the string.
Start three positions before the end and count forward.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The final three characters are OOK.

questions.onCorrect: 3. Starting three back from the end and running to the end takes the last three characters.

misconceptions.feedback: That is where the slice begins when counted from the front. A negative start counts back from the end.

hints: Was the stripped string stored anywhere?
name still refers to its original text.
Count every character in ' bay ', spaces included.
questions.prompt: With name = ' bay ' and the separate line name.strip(), what is len(name)?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: name is unchanged: space, b, a, y, space is five characters.

questions.onCorrect: 5. The stripped string was thrown away, so name still holds the spaces: one, b, a, y, one.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts the stripped text. Nothing stored it, so name is unchanged.

hints: Where does the pencil start, and where does it end?
Length is the distance between the two marks.
Take the start mark away from the end mark.
questions.prompt: How long is the pencil, in centimetres?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The pencil spans from 2 to 5, so 5 − 2 = 3 cm.

questions.onCorrect: 3 cm. The length is the end mark minus the start mark. Slices work the same way: stop minus start.

misconceptions.feedback: That is where the pencil ends on the ruler. Its length is the distance from the tip.
That adds the marks. The length is the gap between them.

hints: Positions are counted as distances from the start.
questions.prompt: Which position holds the first character of a string?
questions.onCorrect: Position 0. Positions count the distance from the start, so the first character is zero steps along.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the second character. Python starts counting at zero.
The last position is reached with a negative number like -1, not the first.

hints: The slice starts four from the end. Where does it naturally finish?
questions.prompt: What does an empty stop in [-4:] mean?

choices.label: Carry on to the end of the string

acceptedIdeas: Carry on to the end of the string
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Without a stop, the slice runs to the end of the string.

questions.onCorrect: An empty stop means carry on to the end of the string.

misconceptions.feedback: Position 0 is the start of the string. A slice going from near the end towards 0 would be empty.
A slice takes everything from the start to the stop, not a single character.

hints: Write out the positions: start at 1.
Stop before you reach 5.
Count 1, 2, 3 and the next one.
questions.prompt: How many positions are there from 1 up to, but not including, 5?

misconceptions.feedback: That counts position 5 too. The stop is not included.
That is 5 − 2. The slice starts at 1, not 2.
